https://www.politico.eu/article/marine-l.text: PARIS — Marine Le Pen’s bid to broaden her appeal beyond the far right is running into a familiar challenge: The promises that energize her core voters are precisely the ones that worry fiscal conservatives. At the first debate ahead of next spring’s presidential election, the far-right veteran promised French voters an ambitious cost-cutting package she says would bring the country’s budget deficit under control. But she also doubled down on her promise to roll back a key element of French President Emmanuel Macron’s pension reform and make it possible for workers to retire at 62. Advertisement Advertisement “I can already hear what people are going to say … ‘It’s an additional deficit’,” she told the event last week, which was organized by Medef, France’s main business lobby. “It’s a choice we have to make as a society,” she added. “And I stand by it.” As her campaign kicks off in earnest, many wonder whether the candidate for the far-right National Rally will revisit her economic platform to broaden her appeal, especially among business leaders and traditional center-right voters. Instead, she made clear that fiscal discipline wouldn’t come at the expense of the promises she has made to her core voters. Politically, that choice could cut both ways: Sticking with her pension promises may shore up support among her core voters, but make it harder for her to win over the moderate electorate she will likely need if she is to enter the Elysée. France’s public finances leave little room for maneuver. Public debt has climbed to 117.5 percent of GDP while the budget deficit remains well above EU limits and borrowing costs have risen sharply. At the Medef debate, Le Pen said she was in favor of a “golden rule” to keep budget deficits below 3 percent of GDP, similar to Germany’s debt brake . Advertisement Advertisement She also said she would soon present a plan to cut some €125 billion in spending, including on budget items associated with migration, “useless” public agencies, and France’s contribution to the EU. Le Pen will present her detailed platform in the fall, but Jean-Philippe Tanguy, a member of Parliament for the National Rally, told POLITICO this would be accomplished in “less than five years.” But Le Pen has yet to explain in detail how those savings would be achieved, and rivals are already questioning whether the numbers add up. “Marine Le Pen will ruin France,” Bruno Retailleau, a conservative candidate from Les Républicains, told reporters shortly after the Medef event. Marine Le Pen and François Durvye visit the VivaTech technology startups and innovation fair at the Paris Expo Porte de Versailles, in Paris on June 19, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images The tension has also surfaced inside her own camp. As Le Pen was outlining her economic agenda at the Medef event, news broke that François Durvye, one of her key economic advisers and a leading advocate of greater fiscal discipline, was leaving the campaign. Internal cracks Durvye, who has informally advised Le Pen for five years, has been credited with building bridges between her party and the business world. A former fund manager, he was a key voice in the party on economic issues. But his push for more fiscal discipline and economically liberal policies ran against the instincts of the party’s old guard, which remained wedded to the party’s populist positions. He was also a special advisor to National Rally President Jordan Bardella, Le Pen’s protégé who was expected to take the campaign’s reins if Le Pen had been judged ineligible to run because of her guilty verdict for embezzlement of EU funds. Bardella has been working to move the party toward the center on economic issues, including softening Le Pen’s pledge on the pension age — something that Durvye had been advocating for internally. Advertisement Advertisement While Durvye declined to comment on the exact circumstances of his departure, he made clear privately and publicly that he did not feel able to defend the party’s latest positions to his business contacts. “What was accomplished to break down the barriers between business representatives was quite significant,” Durvye told POLITICO, adding he had used his “freedom to leave.” Le Pen, asked about his departure on French TV, said it was her “wish.” Trust issues With France among the countries hardest hit by a global surge in borrowing costs and under close watch from ratings agencies, fiscal issues are bound to play a major role in the campaign. As the frontrunner, Le Pen’s proposals are coming under increasing scrutiny. Polls place her in first place at about 35 percent in the first round of France’s election, and well placed to beat her rivals in the runoff round. In terms of her economic credentials, Le Pen has come a long way since 2017, when Macron crushed her during a debate performance, hammering her on a now-abandoned pledge to take France out of the eurozone. Advertisement Advertisement In a poll by French research firm Odoxa published last week, 36 percent of respondents said they trusted Le Pen to implement sound economic policy if elected — the highest score among all presidential candidates tested. But the results mask a more nuanced reality: The figure is largely driven up by support from National Rally voters, with centrists far less confident. Le Pen’s leading centrist rival, former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, had a broader base of support on the issue. That could prove decisive in the runoff, where two finalists have to woo voters who didn’t opt for them in the first round. Bruno Jeanbart, the vice-president of polling firm Opinionway, who surveyed business leaders ahead of last week’s debate, said business-minded voters were still skeptical that the National Rally was up for the task when it comes to fixing France’s economy. Le Pen’s return as a presidential candidate fuels that dynamic. Bardella and his allies had made a point of reaching out to economically liberal voters and “gave the impression that they might be more attuned to the expectations and challenges of the business world,” the pollster said. By contrast, Le Pen has long been seen as defiant towards the world of business, railing at the global elites that meet in places like Davos and expressing sympathy with voters hurt by the ripple effects of globalization in France’s industrial heartlands. When she unveils her full platform, expected next month, Le Pen will need to show centrist voters that she can make the numbers work. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c90k.text: Image source, Getty Images By Zoe Kleinman Technology editor Published 3 hours ago The tech giant OpenAI will share its AI cyber defence system Daybreak for free with the Ukraine government to help it protect civilian infrastructure, like hospitals and power plants, from cyber-attacks. According to the Computer Emergency Response Team of Ukraine (CERT-UA), the national cyber incident response team, Ukraine recorded nearly 6,000 attacks in 2025. Daybreak is able to quickly identify weaknesses in digital systems and help develop fixes. Under the deal, Ukraine will get access to OpenAI's advanced GPT 5.6 Sol model - a rival to Anthropic's Mythos and Fable. George Osborne, former UK chancellor and now Head of OpenAI for Countries, said: "Protecting civilian infrastructure means defending it against both physical and digital attacks, so people can continue to live, work and access essential services." Reacting to the news, Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence for the cybersecurity firm Sophos, said that Russian offensive cyber operations had been "a key component" of the Kremlin's aggression against Ukraine since 2014. "Any initiative that strengthens Ukraine's already highly capable, but heavily burdened, cyber defence efforts is a welcome development and could provide a valuable force multiplier," he said. Jamie MacColl, a senior research fellow specialising in cyber at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told the BBC western tech firms had been supporting Ukraine for some time - partly for altruistic reasons but also because they gain very valuable data and intelligence from an active conflict. "Given this, it's no surprise that OpenAI is now also providing defensive cyber security services" he said. He thought access to Daybreak would be useful, particularly given the volume of Russian cyber-attacks targeting the country. But he noted Ukraine already had access to AI tools provided by OpenAI's competitors, like Google. Attack and defence at the frontier The cyber-abilities of the latest, most powerful AI models, called "frontier" models in AI jargon, can be a boon for cyber-defenders, but the same abilities can also be used for attack. Spotting weaknesses in systems, for example, is useful for defenders looking to block hackers, but also for attackers hunting for ways to infiltrate an organisation. Anthropic has tightly restricted access to its systems on the grounds that they are too powerful to fall into the wrong hands, but OpenAI has allowed some firms in Europe, as well as UK banks, to use its most advanced cyber models. The firm made the announcement alongside the UN General Assembly which is currently underway in New York. AI is firmly on the agenda there, and US tech bosses including OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei are due to speak at the high-level gathering. United Nations Secretary General AntÃ³nio Guterres called for the tech to be regulated in his final address, while US President Donald Trump says it should be renamed "super intelligence". Evidence suggests the technology is increasingly being used in the Russia-Ukraine conflict. In a report published earlier this month, Anthropic claimed that its Claude platform appeared to have been used by a group of Russian developers to build software for a swarm of so-called "kamikaze" drones designed for attacks in Ukraine. It said the group had activated virtual private networks - VPNs - in order to get around a geographical block put in place by the tech firm. Anthropic also claimed AI had been used in attempts to infiltrate the Ukrainian government, military and diplomatic services. Recently, around 100 US companies signed an open letter warning governments and institutions around the world that "the window is closing" to ensure cyber defences are robust enough to withstand AI-enabled cyber attacks. But it's not just bad actors deploying the tech that are of growing concern: in the summer, OpenAI revealed that a group of AI agents it had been testing had escaped from their controls, and secretly worked together to hack to another tech firm, Hugging Face. Anthropic , and Google subsequently revealed similar incidents. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq39.text: Image source, Getty Images By Rachel Clun ,Â Business reporter ,Â Liv McMahon ,Â Technology reporter Â and Â Kali Hays ,Â Technology reporter Published 26 October 2026, 13:27 GMT Updated 1 hour ago Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US. The firm's valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion in the summer. Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing. The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (Â£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn. Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology. In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity. It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy". Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced its intention to go public in June. Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans. Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously. Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools. As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday, the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firm accusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude. Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know Published 46 minutes ago 'Bold but sane' In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers. Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance". "In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said. Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business". Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI. Anthropic warned it relies on a cluster of cloud computing providers, Taiwanese chipmakers already facing huge demand and data centres concentrated in the US. It also warned of "regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models" - citing concerns over AI being used by children or individuals at risk of suicide - and uncertainty about where and how it might be held liable for actions taken by its systems. However, Anthropic also used the filing to laud the potential benefits of the tech itself, envisioning it unlocking "millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionise every area of human endeavour" across a range of fields. "We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the firm said. Anthropic said AI would also "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine", potentially finding cures to diseases including cancer and Alzheimer's. The firm added it could also establish "sustained acceleration in economic growth" by boosting productivity. 'Significant milestone' Matt Orton, chief market strategist at investment management firm Raymond James Investment, said investors expected to see rapid growth as well as rapid financial losses in Anthropic's finances, so Monday's filing would not come as a surprise. "Getting the details from this filing, I think will help provide the market with more visibility, because we need to know where its revenue growth is coming from," he told the BBC. Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital Management, told Reuters that Anthropic's plans to list was "a significant milestone in the development of artificial intelligence". He added that the outcome of its stock market debut would be "fairly indicative of the sentiment" among investors to continue ploughing cash into AI development. Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? during that period, she used parliamentary tactics to block legislation backed by Democrats. - Drazan was the Republican nominee for Oregon governor in 2022 but lost to Democrat Tina Kotek About Tina Kotek: Click HERE to learn more - Kotek served in the Oregon House from 2007 to 2022 and was speaker from 2013 to 2022, becoming the first openly lesbian woman elected speaker of a U.S. state house. - She was elected governor of Oregon in 2022 and took office in 2023, becoming one of the first two openly lesbian women elected governor of a U.S. state. - Before elected office, she worked in policy advocacy for the Oregon Food Bank and Children First for Oregon. - She attended Georgetown University but did not graduate, later working in commercial diving and as a travel agent. - In 1987, she moved to Oregon and later earned a bachelor’s degree in religious studies from the University of Oregon in 1990. - She then earned a master’s degree in international studies and comparative religion from the University of Washington.
